title: The Ansar weep
hookLine: after Hunayn the Ansar feel left out of the gifts, and he tells them: others go home with sheep and camels, and you with the messenger

lines: SOME OF THE YOUNG MEN TALK.
cards: After the battle of Hunayn, there's a great deal to hand out. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gives generously, to leaders from Mecca and the tribes who have only just come over to Islam.
The Ansar, the people of Medina who took him in when he had to leave Mecca, receive nothing from it. They notice. Some of the younger men talk.
He gives to Quraysh, they say, while our swords still drip with their blood. Word reaches him. Today: the Ansar weep.

teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, he doesn't send a message. He gathers the Ansar in one place, just them, and speaks to them directly. First he reminds them of what they've been through together.
Didn't I find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? Divided, and Allah brought you together? In need, and Allah made you rich?

To each line they answer: Allah and His messenger are more generous. Then he turns it around. In Bukhari he tells them that if they wished, they could answer him back: you came to us like this, and like this.
Ibn Ishaq's sirah fills it in: you came to us rejected, and we believed you; alone, and we helped you.

teach.h: HE TELLS THEIR SIDE FOR THEM.
teach.b: He says their side of the story out loud for them.

teach.h: SHEEP AND CAMELS, OR THE MESSENGER.
teach.b: Won't you be content, he asks, that people go home with sheep and camels, and you go home with the messenger of Allah?
If people took one valley and the Ansar another, he would take the valley of the Ansar.

In Ibn Ishaq's sirah, this is where they weep, until their beards are wet, and they say: we're content with the messenger of Allah as our share. One way to read it: the hurt wasn't really about camels.
It was about whether they still mattered to him. So he didn't hand them more goods. He told them, plainly and in front of each other, what they meant to him.
And after the conquest of Mecca, his own city, he went home to Medina with them, and stayed.

how: Muslims retell the Prophet's speech to the Ansar after Hunayn from Sahih al-Bukhari and the sirah, and his words about the valley of the Ansar are quoted when people speak of the bond between him and the people of Medina.

o: the tribes who had only just come over to Islam
the helpers: the people of Medina who took him in
the emigrants who left Mecca for Medina with him

games.q: you're the Prophet. the people who sheltered you feel left out of the gifts. what do you give them?
o: a larger share of the goods.
your words, and yourself: you go home with me.
games.why: he gathered them and asked: won't you be content that others take sheep and camels, and you take the messenger home?

practice: Bring to mind someone who has stood by you without much thanks and might feel a little overlooked: a parent, a friend, a coworker who covers for you.

The way he did, say their side for them, quietly: you were there when I needed you. Then find the one plain sentence you'd want them to hear, not a gift, a sentence; if you pray, you can ask Allah to bless them.

wordCard.voice: Ansar, 'the helpers,' the people of Medina who felt left out of the gifts after Hunayn, until the Prophet told them they would go home with him. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'the helpers', the name for the Muslims of Medina who took in the Prophet and those who emigrated with him.

carryVoice: Your line: you go home with me. Not sheep or camels: him. That's day seven hundred ninety-two.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Ansar's weeping after Hunayn)
